You thought it would hurt the Serb cause because you could tell walking in that those people were being held in unacceptable conditions; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have an argument with Radovan about that. I asked him why we needed all that, and then he told me that he had not done that, that it was some other people over there who --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask you to focus very carefully on my question. You thought it would hurt the Serb cause because you recognised these were unacceptable conditions; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Illegal conditions; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a huge concentration of people in a small space. Illegal, unnatural ... remains to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's discuss it. You know as you sit there today that people were abused, tortured, and murdered in Omarska; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that. I was not even aware of Omarska camp, i.e., collection centre. I was not in the picture at all. When Radovan Karadzic told me that I had to do this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that because I enjoyed reputation, I had authority, then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- I asked you as you sit there today you are aware, aren't you, that people were abused, tortured, and murdered in Omarska. Today.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the conditions were bad. I heard that some people had been killed there. That's all I ever knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if we could have your OTP interview back --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 65 ter 31770, page 42 in the English, and 62 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- you say in your statement and you said -- well, you say in your statement when you're discussing Omarska in paragraph 43 that the local authorities in Prijedor acted on their own initiative. What you said --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What you said in 2001 discussing Omarska --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we're towards the bottom of the page, line 35 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say first: "Radovan Karadzic never told me to get Muslim functionaries or politicians out of there. I did it on my own initiative. What I want to say is that Radovan Karadzic told me personally that he had nothing to do with that but my feeling is what I have is that the order about the camp, about the camps to be established, didn't come from Brdjanin, but somewhere, someone on the top, but I don't know who from." So your opinion expressed in your statement, that the Prijedor authorities acted on their own initiative with regard to the camps, is an opinion you developed between 2001 when you gave this interview and 2013 when you testified in Mr. Karadzic's Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic told me that he had nothing to do with those camps, that some idiots had done that of their own will. He told me of that in this own initiative and that is what I base my position on. Obviously after so many years I have spoken with people and asked them what was going on in Prijedor at the time. I know that people came to me for two --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, when did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke to him, when Sejmenovic was drinking coffee in my office. The door was ajar, the door was open --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So he told you that in 1992. In 2001, you believed that the order had come from above. What I'm putting to you is you've changed your evidence between the interview you gave in 2001 and your testimony on Mr. Karadzic's behalf last year. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is not correct. What I am saying is true. You don't want my truth, do you? So what am I supposed to do? Allow me to tell you the truth. You are the Prosecutor, you represent the United Nations, and you on behalf of the entire globe have to be fair. You represent a serious body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. What Mr. Traldi is exploring at this moment, whether you have been consistent in what you said earlier and what you said later. So if you say I'm telling you the truth, Mr. Traldi is exploring which of the two moments reflects what really is the truth, because he sees some inconsistency in it. That's what he is doing and that's what he's supposed to do. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Leaving Omarska now for Keraterm, you also know as you sit there today that serious crimes including mass killings were committed in Keraterm; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall when you learned about it? During the war or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the war and afterwards. There were articles in the newspapers. And what I read in the newspapers is what I accepted as the truth. I was never in Keraterm myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to Manjaca, where you also were yourself, you went in August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You took several prisoners out of Manjaca. For you to do that, it was necessary for you first to get President Karadzic to pardon them; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then you would forward that pardon to the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic, because his corps had authority over the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While you were at Manjaca, you saw a number of Muslims who were sick or ill, and you warned the VRS officers you saw there that they could be legally responsible for the prisoners' condition; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the officers about the Geneva Conventions and prisoners of war. I warned them what might happen if they did not comply with that, because we were signatories of the Geneva Conventions, i.e., Yugoslavia, the state that had disappeared was a signatory and we adopted its obligations and commitments. I was satisfied with what I saw in Manjaca to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now you came to an answer to the question when you said you were satisfied to a certain extent. To what extent and to what extent you were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To what extent? Can I be allowed to talk about Manjaca and what I saw there? If you won't allow me to say what I want, then I won't. Your Honour, please allow me to say what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm inviting you, as a matter of fact, to tell us what you saw, and let's start with, because you said to some extent you were satisfied, which suggests that in other respects you were not satisfied that it was in line with the Geneva Conventions. And I first would like to invite you to tell us what you saw which you considered not to be in line with the Geneva Conventions, if there was anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seemed to me that there was a lot of people in those buildings. The beds were not beds actually. Those were mattresses on the floor. What else? I inspected the food being prepared, what they were given to eat. I saw that. I noticed a number of people who were sick or so I thought. So I said that an infirmary should be opened there. I asked them if there was a doctor there and they said that there was. I said excellent. I said that an infirmary could be opened. I held speeches before the prisoners in those buildings, and I told them all those are innocent and who had not transgressed the law would be released, and those of you who had committed crimes, you would be held responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you what you saw, not what kind of speeches you delivered. You've answered that question. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 40 in the English and 58 in the B/C/S of this same interview. And actually, it will be at, I think, starting at the very bottom of the previous page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi I'm looking at the clock. I don't know how many questions you would have on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to read this paragraph, ask him to confirm it, and then move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do that and then take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What said in 2001 was -- you were asked about Manjaca: "I didn't know that but it's logical. Let me say something. During that day, when I was there," and that time referring to Omarska, "during one day they were all transferred to Manjaca. I went there the next day immediately on my own initiative."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "I gathered a number of officers. I saw a number of Muslims who were lying, lying, fallen sick or ill, I warned or pointed out to the officers that they could possibly be responsible for that. I said that all prisoners were registered and if they make any mistakes in -- towards the prisoners, they would be -- they would sue or they would be called liable or responsible for it. They were in stables, there was hay under them, and on the hay was one blanket." Do you stand behind the truthfulness and accuracy of that description of what you saw at Manjaca that you provided in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I will turn to new topic after the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break first. Mr. Kupresanin, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. Mr. Traldi, I think your announcement was four hours. Then we are -- there's not much left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I admit I'm running a few minutes behind but expect to be done in the first half of this next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well then, you're not a few minutes behind but quite a bit. Try to -- my record tells me that you have 15 minutes left. Try to see to what extent you can stick to within your time-limits. And if you go over it, it should be minutes, not much more. We take a break and will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, the Chamber suggested that we would proceed and that any e-court problem you're suffering from at this moment will be fixed. If that causes you real problems then, of course, we would stop and wait until everything is done, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to the massacre at Brisevo in Prijedor municipality. You do not mention this in your statement but you have been interviewed about it. Now, you went to Brisevo yourself in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to Brisevo. I did attempt to enter it, unsuccessfully though. I still can't explain to myself why. In any case, I met the wives of those killed in Brisevo and I spoke with them. We were in a small Catholic church. Later on, there was a mass led by the Archbishop Komarica. All of the women present asked for my help. They asked me to help them to leave the village and to secure buses for them to go on to a number of European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to go step by step through your evidence about this. You say you went with Bishop Komarica. You went with him and two VRS officers from the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you spoke to the gathering of Croat survivors that you described; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the Croat women who were there. There were no men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They told you that there had been a massacre in --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They told you the VRS had entered the village and killed 68 people and destroyed a large number of houses; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that the Army of Republika Srpska -- actually not the Army of Republika Srpska but that somebody enter the village and killed a number of people. I don't know whether they said 60 or 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 63 in the English, 92 in the B/C/S, of this same interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There's a big buzz coming from the English both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we were bothered by some buzz, but it came in and went out again and if there's -- let's see whether we can get rid of it forever. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, for context let's have the bottom of the previous page, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you were asked: "Did you know who was responsible for the [sic] crimes in Brisevo?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we then turn to the next page in the English. And you answered: "Well, they said that it was committed by, the crimes were committed by the army. That they, they did it suddenly, quickly, very quickly, in a flash light." Does that refresh your recollection as to whether you were aware that it was specifically the VRS that had committed those crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a conversation with the officers later on, they said that it wasn't the army, that it was no military operation. They said that -- a group of people did that of their own initiative and for their own reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, first, you didn't mention that in 2001 in your interview, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what I said in 2001. Perhaps you can read it back to me. What I saw is what I'm telling you now. Perhaps there may be some differences in details between my statement and now because of the time which has elapsed, but what I'm telling you is true. I keep appealing to the truth being heard before the UN, but it seems you're very unwilling to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you refrain from these kind of comments. We are asking questions. We are carefully listening to your answers. But we have -- there were some moments of perceived inconsistencies, there were movements of perceived contradictions, and they have to be clarified. That does not justify any comment that Mr. Traldi or anyone else in this courtroom would not be willing to hear the truth. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, what I'm suggesting to you, sir, is that between your interview in 2001 you seem to have forgotten a number of things and recalled a number of others, and the things that you have -- that you claim to have recalled in the intervening time all, I suspect, you believe diminish the responsibility of President Karadzic and General Mladic for the crimes that you discussed in your interview, and I put to you that your testimony today is not truthful. Do you have any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that it was not a planned military operation. In my conversations with different people, I managed to establish that. It turned out that a group of soldiers committed what they did. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is again a problem and the English booth is blamed for it, at least that it comes from the English booth. Could we have the assistance of technicians so that where the English booth, I think ... Oh, technicians are looking at it at this moment. But the English booth is innocent until proven guilty. Please proceed. Witness, again, you're not responding to the question that is put to you. The question is that there are differences between your previous statements and your present statements, what -- and your later evidence. Mr. Traldi puts it to you that the things you have forgotten and the things you have now remembered, that they -- he understands them to be not totally impartial. He said that the responsibility of President Karadzic and Mladic, through the new version, is lowered, and he puts to you that that is what you intend to do, to tell us a story which is more favourable to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic. That's what he asks you. Please respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel very uncomfortable using more time at this trial than necessary. I am not an attorney and, of course, mistakes are possible. However, what I know is what I said just a moment ago. It was not a military operation. There was a group of soldiers who did that and the problem was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness -- okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only add to my previous opinion: If in 2001 I said something, I could have been wrong. If I learned something afterwards in terms of truth, why would I not be allowed to amend my original statement in order to arrive at a complete rather than partial truth. And please help me out with that. The whole truth is that these soldiers killed civilians, males, they committed a crime, and it is true that they were not held responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are misunderstanding what your role is. You're invited to tell us what the women told you. If someone else told you something else later, you can tell us as well. Mr. Traldi then asks why you didn't tell it at the time when you were interviewed, but let's leave all that alone. Finally, who is telling the truth, ladies or military officers that you spoke with later on, that's not for you to draw conclusions from what you heard. What we want to know is what did the women tell you, and if you say I heard something else from someone else, fine, tell us what they told us, but don't present your conclusions in this respect as the truth. Tell us who told you what. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just briefly to follow up. The Chamber has received evidence, I believe it's P2440 but I'll double-check the reference, that that was, in fact, a military operation directed at villages in Prijedor including Brisevo at the time those crimes were committed. You weren't part of the operation and you don't know whether there was or wasn't, do you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are two questions, Mr. Traldi. The first one is you did not participate in that military operation, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the -- the second question was that you don't know what happened exactly in this military operation. You have no personal knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what you heard about this crime, you didn't keep to yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question before you go to that step. Sir, you say -- what you heard was that these were just soldiers who were doing this and it was not a military operation. But on this statement that is -- Mr. Traldi is quoting you from, you say: "I didn't say anything. I don't know, I really don't know. They said," now these are the women, "that the VRS army barged in. I didn't which brigade. You know what? Those subjects and topic at the beginning of the war, it was very dangerous to reveal them or uncover them. Many people even if they heard that, they didn't want to hear it, about it." Do you have any comment on that statement, that the VRS barged in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I've nothing to say. I don't know who broke into the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, you have answered my question. Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't keep what you learned about the crime that had been committed there to yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't keep it for myself. Why I would have gone there if I had wanted to keep it all for myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You told, for instance, Momcilo Krajisnik, the president of the assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I did speak with Komarica and a number of officers regarding the fate of the women in Brisevo. Our thinking was along the lines that they should be allowed to go because of everything they had gone through in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look now at the bottom of page 91 of this same interview in the B/C/S and page 62 in the English. And beginning at line 43 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were asked -- you say: "Well, what I heard there I told to others. It didn't stay with me ..." You were asked: "Who did you inform, who did you inform?" And you say: "For example, Momo Krajisnik, maybe a certain numbers of minister, all deputies from here ..." That's the truth what you said there, that you told, among others, Momcilo Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said perhaps. I don't know who I informed specifically. I don't remember that. I did inform someone, but I don't know who exactly. Maybe I even informed the radio. I'm not sure who I told. In any case, what I had promised I saw it done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, in that interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First I would like to draw the witness's attention to the fact that he didn't say "perhaps." You said: "For example, Momo Krajisnik." Can you look at the transcript of your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same or similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't decided on a particular person. I said that perhaps I did inform someone. But it wasn't so important for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was important for me to -- was to see through the promise I had given to the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the fact that you now gave a different account. In the interviews, then you said, "for example," which is not the same as "perhaps." Now you are saying "perhaps." If you say "for example," then it is a clear statement that you did it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was expected of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's all fine. What Judge Fluegge is doing is to clearly put to you that you -- when you said, I said "perhaps," that at least on the record, on the transcript of your interview, you did not say "perhaps." If you say it's unimportant for me or it's all the same, that's a different matter, but that's not what you are recorded to have said. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Continuing with this topic, and I'm going to return to the approach of simply reading you portions of this interview, you were asked a couple of lines later: "The officers from the 1st Krajina Corps, they were also present when you were being informed?" You respond: "Yes, they were always present." Do you stand behind the truthfulness and accuracy of your statement at the time that the officers from the 1st Krajina Corps were always present when you were informed about the crimes that had been committed in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were our guarantee for myself and for Archbishop Komarica. It was war time and whenever one would see a vehicle with officers, it indicated caution for the sake of our safety, and to reduce the level of risk they accompanied us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next page, that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- next page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Continuing with the topic of who you informed, we see here, beginning at line 6 in the B/C/S and 29 in the English that you confirm to the people of Brisevo: "I said that I would probably inform the military leadership or something. I probably informed Mladic about it, now I can't remember." That was what you said in 2001, that you believed you'd probably informed General Mladic himself; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. As far as I recall, I informed Talic rather than Mladic. I also informed a number of officers from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, on this same page, you were being asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we go back now to the previous page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're being asked when they told you soldiers from the VRS were involved in the crimes, did it occur to you that you should inform General Talic about it, and you said no. So I'd put to you that when you were interviewed in the context of the Talic trial, you say: "No, I didn't tell Talic but I probably told Mladic," and when you testify in the Mladic trial, you say: "No, I didn't tell Mladic, but I probably told Talic." I'd put to you that you are not being truthful with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have the next page in B/C/S so the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a matter not for re-examination, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it would be too late now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- because we have recorded words of this witness on this topic exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, should we -- should the witness listen to this at this moment or should he take his earphones off. Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Kupresanin, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I found in B/C/S and I have to find it in English to read it to you, but in B/C/S it's on this page in front of us, line 7. Although mentioning the name of General Mladic, it is recorded "but I cannot remember now."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I read that out. I also read that before that he said I probably informed General Mladic. I gave the full context of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "But I cannot remember now," so he couldn't remember then. So he's not changing. He just mentioned the name, but he said "I cannot remember now."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. That was read to him. And at least the witness is asked to comment on that, and it's perfectly a matter which you could deal with in re-examination because Mr. Traldi did not unfairly read, I think, the various versions the witness gave about events. But let me check that very carefully. Could you assist me, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the same page in English. It's line 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now. It's -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the transcript of today, page 63, lines 18 and 19, Mr. Traldi said, quoted "I probably informed Mladic about it, now I can't remember." It's part of the quote that Mr. Traldi read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was fairly read to the witness. Now the next question is whether it's summarised well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Claiming that he is changing something now is not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, probability -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He expressed a probability at that moment, whether that's very wise to seek probabilities in a witness interview is another matter. But then -- let me ... Yes, I think it's -- page 64, Mr. Traldi puts to the witness that when he was interviewed, that he said: I didn't tell Talic but I probably told Mladic. Well, if you know for sure you do not say I probably told Mladic. Then you say, I told Mladic. So at that moment, he expressed both a probability and that he doesn't clearly remember. The two can exist next to each other the one does not invalidate the other. If I say I probably went there but I don't know for sure, then there must be a reason on my mind why I think that I went there rather than to a totally different place even if I do not fully remember. There's nothing in what Mr. Traldi did which is not fair to the witness. And second, it is a matter which you could have dealt with in re-examination. But, Mr. Lukic, if it is your view, of course you can explore that with the witness, that if someone says this is what probably happened but I don't remember, that it means that he still thinks it's a probability but he can't say it for sure. That is a situation which doesn't need further explanation. We'll just move on. Could the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to articulate what you're now trying to object to which is what Mr. Traldi said. Mr. Traldi said when you testified in the Talic case you said you probably told Mladic. Today you are testifying in the Mladic case. You are now saying you probably told Talic and this is what this witness has said today. In this report, he says he probably told Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- I think we unanimously agree that nothing was done wrong. Could the witness put on his earphones again. And Mr. Traldi may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just checking whether the question was answered. It was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then, sir, I'll ask the question again. I'd put to you that when you were interviewed in the context of the Talic trial, you said, no, I didn't tell Talic but I probably told Mladic. And when you testify in the Mladic trial, you say, no, I didn't tell Mladic, but now I recall that I told Talic, and I'd put to you that you are not being truthful with this Tribunal. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember who I informed at this time. I said perhaps and it was to be expected that the top of the army be informed. I don't know who I informed specifically. There's no written trail, and I'm not sure I did inform anyone in a written form. In any case, the operation was over. In my mind, it was successful. Now who I informed is something I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One reason that it was to be expected that the top of the army would be informed was that the officers who were there with you audio recorded the meeting where the Croat women told you what had happened; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their own task, these officers. Perhaps. I do not want to discuss their tasks, but I presume they must have had one. I don't think they were simply driving us around. They were monitoring the situation. I wanted to remind you that I did not manage to get into Brisevo although I wanted to. We were simply unable to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the bottom of this same page, you were asked: "So, you're saying that whatever was said in Brisevo, in that gathering, the military officers, they were video recording everything?" You say: "No." You were asked: "So, how were they recording it?" You say: "What do you call it, something like this?" And you were asked: "Oh, you mean audio recording?" And you say: "Just sound." Do you stand by that portion of your interview as accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just assume so. I didn't see a dictaphone. I just assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, like several other pages, I haven't always said it, but we'll seek to add that to P6994 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear that whatever subject you deal with in this interview that it will be considered for selection to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Before finishing the Brisevo topic, sir, you knew that Brisevo had been an unarmed village and there was no combat there; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything. I didn't even know which municipality Brisevo was in. Even now I don't know whether it belongs to Prijedor or Sanski Most. It was an area that I didn't know about. I just responded to a request by Komarica. I went to look at the situation. Anywhere I was asked, I would go. I tried to resolve these things with Komarica and with the leadership of the municipality. I was there, I was in Sasina...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 31772.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a portion of the re-examination that Mr. Karadzic conducted, so he's asking you the questions. And he says, beginning at line 4: "Brisevo was mentioned. Was Brisevo an undefended village with civilians that some armed formation of the Serbs attacked? Was there any combat there or was this an unarmed village? " And you say: "I think it was unarmed. There was no combat there." Do you stand by the truthfulness and accuracy of this portion of your testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I stand by it. It was not armed. Even a number of villagers from the village were in the Army of Republika Srpska and that is why I'm wondering a lot why this was said: A military operation on an unarmed village. I mean, it's not logical. It could have been just a whim of individuals from the Army of Republika Srpska. That is something that can be discussed, but I don't know what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution have 65 ter 31769 and this will be the last document I use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, as it comes up this will a letter from Bishop Komarica to yourself. Aside from Brisevo, he informed you of a number of other massacres of Croat civilians in Sanski Most, Kotor Varos, and elsewhere in the ARK; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I do remember the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And directing your attention to point 1, we see he refers to massacres of civilians in Sanski Most, Skrljevita and other villages, in Bascina, in Kotor Varos, and Ljubija in Prijedor. Turning to page 2 in both languages, he mentions in this document also the mining and burning of Catholic churches, the razing of houses and other properties. And just before point 2, he informs you: "Unfortunately, the general result is still quite negative resulting in almost horrific massive evacuation by my faithful, especially from the Sanski Most and Prijedor regions, in an effort to save their bear lives." Did the information that Croats were fleeing Sanski Most and Prijedor in order to save their bear lives remain with you or did you also pass that on to the military and other Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that Mr. Komarica informed only me about it. I think he informed others and other institutions. What Mr. Komarica asked me to do, I implemented in the field in Banja Luka. I always had the bishops, the hodzas, the president of the SDA, the president of the HDZ in my office constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going ask you two specific questions. Did you inform the 1st Krajina Corps command of these crimes that Bishop Komarica informed you of?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Banja Luka Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska was informed about it, they knew about it, they went with me to visit all those places. It was only Brisevo. I went with Komarica to all the places where Croats were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you inform the Republika Srpska government of the crimes against Croats that he informed you of, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Bishop Komarica informed the president of the republic, and I don't know if he informed General Mladic and the president of the assembly. That is something that I don't know. And I know that that president, the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, responded to them, saying you can contact Vojo. That was the most frequent, let's say, instruction or directive that Radovan would give out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Bishop Komarica says in this letter that there are horrific massive evac indications by Croats from the ARK. You were aware, you and the other members of the political leadership in the ARK, that Muslims and Croats were fleeing the area in large numbers; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of those cases in Sanski Most and in Prijedor. I knew these things were happening. I went to the field. It's not true that there was an exodus of Muslims and Croats and that I didn't notice that. There was an exodus but what it was was that people were fleeing from those villages and from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination and I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31769 receives exhibit number P7011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness -- to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kupresanin, good day once again.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a lot of topics that I would like to cover, a lot of documents that we need to look at, so I would just like you to gather your strength.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to start with Thursday. My colleague, Mr. Traldi, asked you about logistical support received by the Army of Republika Srpska through the Main Staff from Serbia. On page 29679 of our transcript, line 19, is where there is this assertion made. Did the Army of Republika Srpska ask the Crisis Staff of the ARK to supply them with food, clothing? Did it make such requests to the municipalities? In practice, how did this look? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, you're invited to slow down in speaking. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the departure of the Yugoslav People's Army from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was in late April and in the course of May, sometime the 20th of May, the state army left, meaning that the Serb people found themselves in an unpleasant situation. They didn't have paramilitary formations, they did not have reserve army troops. Those that they looked to and had hoped for help from had left them and abandoned them. Then we formed our own army on the 12th of May. The army that we formed, and the state was not formed yet, the operational organs did not function yet or the army ministry, so the logistics fell to the municipalities so that the Banja Luka Corps was mostly financed by the municipality of Banja Luka, and the other units were formed -- were financed and supported by other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And throughout the war, did the municipalities continue to equip, feed the units that were on their territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only to feed and clothe, but I know that the municipalities set aside some funds for the purchase of weapons that we didn't have; for ammunition and so on. All of this was financed by the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next question, the next topic that you were asked about by my colleague Mr. Traldi, on page 29680 of our transcript, lines 20 on, is that the Army of Republika Srpska had a massive advantage in weaponry, and you confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I haven't completed putting my question to you. In your opinion, could Serbs have taken the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said openly at the assembly when the question was asked why does the Army of Republika Srpska not capture all of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that we could finish the war, join Serbia, and avoid all of this. What's happening is senseless. We can cover Bosnia easily so why don't we do that? I claim that we could have done that. When I sought an answer, when I received an answer, then they said, the political leadership said that this was not our objective. Our objective is to protect the Serbian people. The Army of Republika Srpska was perhaps the fourth largest army in Europe or the third largest, or the fifth largest. I mean, you can imagine what that meant in terms of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You meant the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you know what the weapons factories were and the weapons depots that remained in the territory under the control of Bosnian and Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please begin his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness. Could you -- could you re-start. It's a bit unclear to us, but the interpreters asked us whether you could start your answer. So could you re-start your answer to that question about weapon factories and weapon depots, that remained in the territory under the control of the Bosnian and Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I begin? As far as I know, the bulk of the factories were on the side of the Bosnian -- actually, the Muslim Croatian side. The biggest such factory, VBR and tank parts and cannon parts was located in Travnik. It remained in the Federation territory. Konjic manufactured ammunition. It also remained in the B and H federation. Vitez manufactured dynamite, Trotyl, explosive materials. Its was in the B and H federation. I think that in Gorazde also there was a bullet factory. I don't know what was left over for Republika Srpska. It was one factory called Kosmos and it was operating in Banja Luka. As far as I know, perhaps that's it. Maybe there was some other things. I think the sniper factories ZRAK in Sarajevo also functioned there. I think we only had one factory on our side. I mean, it's not my intention to make mistakes, but this is -- this is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us this. You mentioned the ZRAK factory in Sarajevo. On whose side was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the Muslim side. It's a sniper factory, precise weapons factory. High-precision weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P6994, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your interview to which my colleague Mr. Traldi referred to often today. It's been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should have called it up by its 65 ter number, 31770. [In English] If we can have B/C/S version on our screens as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know which document I'm talking about. I just want to show you the document and so a few things were put to you in relation to this document. Among other things, towards the end of his cross-examination my colleague, Mr. Traldi, put to you that you provided one statement -- or that this statement, actually, was taken in the context of the Talic trial and that later you testified in the Karadzic and Mladic cases. At this time, when you gave this statement, are you able to remember today if anybody ever told you that they were taking this statement in the context of the General Talic trial?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never discussed the topic of General Talic with any investigator. It's just an empty space, a blank, as far as General Talic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, inter alia, you mentioned here that General Talic or one of his deputies was at meetings. You said that on page 29684, line 15. You said if general was not there, one of his deputies would be.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you also told us that you saw General Talic only once at a Crisis Staff meeting. Those people who deputised for General Talic, were they able to vote, did they have the decision-making power at the Crisis Staff meeting? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I remember one of his deputies who came instead of him. I know that I saw Talic only once. I know that he spoke about bad food in the army, that all the troops were getting was rice, that they were not trained. He asked for the food funds which would make all of us safe. The person who deputised for him did not vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to talk about the topic of regionalisation. You were shown a document by my learned friend Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number is P6995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document was issued on the 25th September. You will see it on the screen shortly. 25th September 1991 is the date on the document. It was suggested to you that the ARK was established based on this decision, just like all the other SAOs.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Bear with me. In September, on the 25th September when this document was passed or perhaps even -- even the 7th of September, 1991, and this document refers to that date, had ARK already functioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1991. Was it set up before, did it function?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was sometime at the end of August or the beginning of September the Assembly of Republika Srpska abolished regions. It is not that I believe that. I'm sure of that. It was either in Doboj or Bijeljina. It was sooner in Bijeljina. But in any case, from then onwards, the regions no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to avoid confusion in the record, if we could get a time-period for the -- specifically a year for the answer that the witness has just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard my learned friend, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was in 1991 either at the end of August or beginning of September. That's when the regions disappeared, i.e., the Assembly of Republika Srpska abolished those regions sometime around that time, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we discussed D853, which is the transcript of the founding Assembly of ARK, it is not clear from the document when that assembly meeting took place. However, on page 29665 of our transcript to a question put to you by Judge Orie on line 5, you answered that that meeting was held on the 24th April 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is -- we have to see the next document, which is 65 ter 16110.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, dated 14 May 1992, which is the minutes of the 2nd Session of the Assembly of the Association of Bosnian Krajina, that precedes the SAO founding document by approximately three months. We can see that ARK is functioning. My question is this:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I object to the characterisation. It's quite clear we're conflating the ZOBK and the ARK in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, but the objection is that in the introduction to this question, you're mixing up matters. Could you either demonstrate that you are not or rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when did the Association of the Municipality of Bosanska Krajina become a region? Did the same people continue to work in it?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was sometime in August, but I'm not sure. It may have been that I am not telling the truth. The same bodies continued to exist. Why they changed the name? Because of the attribute or the region with the Serbian attribute had already been set up, the Serbian SAO, we had the Serbian Autonomous Region. In order to avoid the attribute "Serbian" and for all the people who resided in that area to be calmer and to feel better, to have a region belong to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said August, what year were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps 1991; but, again, I'm not sure. If I make a mistake it's not intentional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have just one more question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that before the war?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Much before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes when you said that you would have one more question, it was just before the break and not in your re-examination. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Traldi always makes us work a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you trigger that yourself as well, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I have to cover many documents, and I think that there were conflicting evidence and conflicting statements, and I have to clarify many, many things with this witness. I tried to object at some points. Some points I didn't even object. But I'll have to cover many topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider that. We'll -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One brief matter before the break, but we don't need the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't need the witness. Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just in light of some of the questions early on in redirect, we have reviewed the transcript of the interview and I'd direct Mr. Lukic's attention to pages 74 and 75 where Mr. Kupresanin was directly informed that it was in the context of the Brdjanin and Talic investigation. We will seek to have that included as part of the selection of pages from P6994 when we eventually make a selection to propose for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's at the end, actually, or in the middle of this. Not at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the end in the English. And, sorry, it will be at the end in both languages. I just don't have the B/C/S page number ready to hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll take a break, and we will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00. Mr. Stojanovic has an issue to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a very practical issue. Can we instruct the next witness to go back to the hotel or to stay here and wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having listened to Mr. Lukic, there's no -- there's no reason for him to wait because I do understand that there's no way that he would start giving his testimony today, assuming that the Chamber follows you. Well, whatever time you would need, the Chamber would like to instruct the -- in this case, the Defence, that the witness should not remain stand by for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I'd like to put clearly on the record what triggered the removal of Mr. Mladic from the courtroom. When the witness, although not triggered by the question, expressed himself, among other matters, that the Serbian people has reason to be grateful to the general, referring to General Mladic, he -- the accused started applauding aloud and that was the reason for the Chamber to remove him from the courtroom. He has been instructed several times not to intervene in whatever way with the testimony of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Lukic will now continue his re-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And before I continue, I would just kindly ask to make correction on the page 78, line 15, it was in connection with my question. The year mentioned is 1992 and should be 1991, but I think that everybody understood about which document I was speaking since we had it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kupresanin, now I'm going to ask you about P77001B [as interpreted] this is a Prosecutor's document. It is a video-clip in which Smiljko Sagolj reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should repeat the number. I think we are not up to 77001.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Huh? I don't -- okay. It's P7001 [Interpretation] It's P7001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say P7001B?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the document before us. It says in the document that Mr. Radovan Karadzic said: "We no longer have no obligations towards the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina but towards the constitution of Yugoslavia which guarantees our right to self-determination and self-organising for the people." This is a report on the plebiscite of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember whether before that date, representatives of Muslims and Croats in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a declaration of some sort contrary to the will of the Serbian people and contrary to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. It -- the reasons and the terms were not founded, and it was about the reason for the beginning of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One reason was the Islamic declaration by Alija Izetbegovic. That was a political platform. Every political party had its intentions and -- every political party had its intentions. It is true of every political party which appears on the scene in any state. They have their objective and their platform, and from the platform of any political party you can tell exactly what they want. The Serbian Democratic Party had its own platform or program.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I need to interrupt you now. Did you ever hear of the declaration on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was on the 14th October 1991 when a group of deputies, not all the deputies but only the Croatian and Muslim deputies, sometime late in the night - after midnight, that is - together voted on the declaration of -- on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They did it on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please slow down, sir. Please slow down. The interpreters are struggling to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of October, 1991, in the small hours of the night, after midnight, Croatian and Muslim deputies unbeknownst to the Serbian deputies, met after midnight in the building of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and passed this declaration on sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. By doing that, they breached the federal constitution, the republican constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we interrupt you for a second. The events in the assembly on the 14th and 15th October have been dealt with in quite some detail. Mr. Lukic, if there's anything which this witness would add to that, to what is already in evidence, you're invited to put focused questions to him, because it seems that to hear all what happened there again would result in repetitious evidence, and I think - I'm also looking at the Prosecution - that on the main factual part, that perhaps there's no great disagreement. I am not talking about how it's appreciated. But that's, of course, a different matter. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you personally perceive that declaration on independence?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The declaration on independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign, integral, and indivisible state of Bosnia-Herzegovina first humiliated all of us deputies in the assembly and the Serbian people as a whole. Second of all, it broke up Bosnia-Herzegovina. And thirdly, Bosnia-Herzegovina was left there without the Serbian people and the territory where 62 per cent of the Serbian people resided. The Serbian people established its own assembly to cover the political interests of the Serbian people. It organised protection for the Serbian people and that's how Bosnia-Herzegovina imploded and was split into the two entities that would later on be recognised by the Dayton agreement. The Serbian people is a constituent people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state forming people. There are three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the passing of that declaration of independence by the Muslim and Croatian deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you think or believe that it was possible to continue honouring commitments toward the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment Bosnia-Herzegovina imploded. The constitution was made null and void. For the declaration to be passed, two thirds of a majority in Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly had to vote in favour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down. Could the witness please repeat the figures again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are again invited to slow down because the interpreters cannot follow you. Could you re-start. You said two-thirds of a majority in Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly had to vote in favour. And could you resume from there, when you mentioned apparently numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina had 240 members. There were 84 Serb assemblymen, if there were fewer of us, 80 or 79, then the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been honoured. As things stood tendentiously and under the influence of the international community, they did what they did. Bosnia-Herzegovina thus was destroyed through the constitution and after that it has never become united. That's why we had two entities and the Serbian people still need to find their own space in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I believe that that was not done only by Bosnia-Herzegovina on its own. It was done under the pressure of the international community. In December 1991, the Holy City --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, first of all, your question and how the witness perceived all that, and he moves away, far away, from what the question is. So please try to put as focused questions as you can and stop the witness immediately once he moves away from your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My impression was that now are you. You took over from me. And I didn't want to interrupt. But I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked him to re-start his answer at the request of the interpreters, so if -- this is certainly not to be understood as taking over. But I should think about my reputation in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I'll move onto another document. Can we please have P7005.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to make a link between the declaration of independence and the referendum I am about to ask you, tell us please what happened in December 1991? What were you trying to tell us, but briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness started to tell us something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said in order to make a link between this and that, and that is leading because that suggests that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll leave December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a link does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will leave December completely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let's go to the end of February and the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But don't give the context in which the witness has to link matters together. But, meanwhile, I use the opportunity. I understood that the microphone in the English booth was replaced but we have a similar sound now. So could our technicians either find another microphone or do something else to fix it. Meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before us is the stenographic record of the 8th Session of the SN, which probably stands for the Serbian people, dated 25th of February, 1992. As regards evidence in this case, it happened four days before the referendum. Do you know when the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in September although I don't recall exactly. In any case, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told -- do you agree -- as a matter of fact, maybe I should start my question like this: According to what you know at that time you were a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did the Muslim and Croatian representatives in the assembly know, were they informed that the Serbs were opposed to the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they knew. But irrespective of that, I wanted to return to what I initially wanted to say. It wasn't the Serb, Bosniaks, and Croats who started the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, you're supposed to answer a question and not to say this is my answer, and now I'll continue what I want to tell you. You're here to answer questions. Mr. Lukic, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document you were quoted as having said the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 60 in the B/C/S and 75 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you can see, you have the B/C/S version in front of you that you can follow. Actually, this is not the page. My notes about the pagination must be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Traldi in any way in a position to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It depends if you wanted to have the English page on the screen. If that is the right one, then B/C/S is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in English, it's page 75 out of 77, which suggests that you should, in B/C/S, try to find in the very last few pages, and it's 95 pages all together, and ... unless it's ... Could it be page 93 where I see Mr. Kupresanin mentioned at least in the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I have wrong page numbers, I really apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it not the one on our screen now, 93?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But it -- unless the two documents are not completely translated, if it is two pages from the finish in English, then it should not be more than two or three pages from the end in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The whole day we have a problem with electronics and it's not working again so I cannot check it. We tried to solve it during the break but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you had two different pages on the screen. Were you looking for the B/C/S one which was on the screen or the English one which was one the screen previously. You asked for page 60 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that the right one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: None of these pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: None of these pages? Then you should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both English and B/C/S are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I can't assist you. Then you have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But thank you anyways. If we can have P7006, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked about this document. It is an excerpt from the minutes of the 14th Session of the ARK Assembly. My learned friend Mr. Traldi asked you, at page 29740 of our transcript -- well, I believe it requires further explanation, but I'll read out my colleagues question in English so that it is interpreted for you. It is in line 13 and 14 of page 29740. [In English] I quote: "Now, in the days between the 25th and the 29th of February, the constitution had been promulgated; right?"

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were shown this document regarding the issue. In your replies, on page 29742, line 13, you said: [In English] "Only Assembly of Republika Srpska could adopt such constitution." [Interpretation] And at page 29743, line 7, you said: [In English] "I would not be a position to sign a document adopting the republican constitution." [Interpretation] In this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we require the next page, in both versions, that is to say, the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In item 1, we read the following: "The deputies of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina fully accepted the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." You said that you were not in a position to put a constitution into force and that is normal. We had a judge participate in that discussion agreed, and he said that he was asking about facts. Do you recall - if you don't, just say so - why was it necessary for the ARK Assembly to fully accept the constitution of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I am a bit embarrassed. The constitution in the Assembly of Republika Srpska and the MPs who were invited to establish the state were asked to put a constitution into force. They were not duty-bound -- well, they could assume a position given the fact that they had previously read the constitution and they were familiar with the subject matter, then they could perhaps decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Decide what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the end of our working day and I'm finished with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us: They could decide, they could decide what? Witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, what am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said that they could assume a position, having read the constitution, and they were familiar with the subject matter, and then "they could perhaps decide." Decide what, or decide on what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could not decide. I was referring to those who can enact a constitution and who is familiar with it. As for the assembly of the region, I don't know what kind of decision they could make and they did not. They had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm puzzled by the fact that in your previous answer you said "then they could perhaps decide." So you consider it there possible. But now you say it's -- you don't know what kind of a decision they could make. That's still puzzling. But we adjourn for the day. Mr. Lukic, any time estimate for tomorrow, assuming that e-court is functioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid a bit more than first session. Because I just covered Thursday and I have to cover today's day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this is -- let's further discuss this because you know that the number of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try because we are in a rush with the next witness, he has to leave, and I will try to cut it down as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll wait and see. Mr. Kupresanin, we'll conclude your testimony tomorrow but we'll adjourn now for the day. I'd like to instruct you again - as I did last Thursday - that you should not communicate in whatever way, with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. You may follow the usher. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 16th of December, 9.30 in the morning same courtroom, I.
